flashcards.q: Derive Naive Bayes' MAP decision rule and state the independence assumption.
flashcards.a: P(c|d) = P(d|c)P(c)/P(d); since P(d) is constant across classes, pick class maximizing P(d|c)P(c). Naive assumption: P(d|c) = Π P(w_i|c) -- every word conditionally independent given class. False for language, but only the RANKING between classes needs to be right, not the individual probabilities.

flashcards.q: What is the Laplace smoothing formula for Naive Bayes and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: P(w|c) = (count(w,c) + α) / (Σcount(w',c) + α*V). Without it, any word absent from a class's training data gets P(w|c)=0, zeroing the entire product-based likelihood for any test document containing that word.

flashcards.q: Multinomial vs Bernoulli Naive Bayes: what does each model and when does Bernoulli win?
flashcards.a: Multinomial models word frequency (counts); standard for most text classification. Bernoulli models only presence/absence, discarding frequency; can outperform Multinomial on short documents where mere presence carries most of the signal and counts are sparse/noisy.

flashcards.q: Logistic regression vs linear SVM for text classification: what do they optimize and what's the calibration difference?
flashcards.a: LogReg minimizes cross-entropy on a sigmoid output, natively producing P(c|d). Linear SVM minimizes hinge loss, maximizing margin, and does NOT natively produce a calibrated probability -- needs Platt scaling as an extra step.

flashcards.q: Why should multi-label classification use independent sigmoids instead of softmax?
flashcards.a: An item can belong to zero, one, or many labels simultaneously. Softmax forces outputs to sum to 1, enforcing mutual exclusivity that doesn't exist and actively fighting the training signal whenever multiple labels are simultaneously true. Use K independent sigmoids with per-label binary cross-entropy instead.

flashcards.q: What is focal loss and how does it differ from class weighting?
flashcards.a: FL(p_t) = -(1-p_t)^γ * log(p_t), γ≈2. Down-weights easy/confidently-correct examples (p_t→1 shrinks the loss toward 0) regardless of class frequency -- reweights by DIFFICULTY. Class weighting reweights by FREQUENCY (weight_c = N/(K*n_c)), a static, different mechanism; often combined with focal loss.

flashcards.q: Why is accuracy a misleading metric under severe class imbalance, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: A model predicting the majority class for everything can score 95%+ accuracy on a 95/5 split while catching zero minority-class examples. PR-AUC and per-class precision/recall/F1 replace it; ROC-AUC is also misleading since its FPR axis stays deceptively good against a huge negative class.

flashcards.q: What does it mean for a classifier to be calibrated, and are accuracy and calibration the same property?
flashcards.a: Calibration means predicted probability matches empirical correctness frequency -- among 0.9-confidence predictions, roughly 90% should actually be correct. They are independent properties: a highly accurate model can still be badly overconfident (Guo et al. 2017 showed modern neural nets typically are).

flashcards.q: What is temperature scaling and what does it NOT fix?
flashcards.a: Divides pre-softmax logits by a single learned scalar T>1 before softmax, smoothing the output distribution to counteract overconfidence; T is fit by minimizing NLL on a held-out set. It does NOT change accuracy or ranking, and can't fix non-uniform miscalibration (overconfident at high confidence, underconfident at low) since it's a single global parameter -- isotonic regression handles that case instead.

flashcards.q: What does a fine-tuned transformer buy over a linear TF-IDF classifier, mechanically, and at what cost?
flashcards.a: Contextual representation via attention -- captures negation scope, long-range dependency, sarcasm-adjacent context that bag-of-words structurally discards. Cost: single-digit to tens of ms/doc on GPU vs sub-ms to few-ms for linear models on CPU -- a real infrastructure cost at scale, worth paying only when the task has genuine contextual ambiguity and the gap is measured, not assumed.

flashcards.q: What's a cascade architecture for balancing classification cost and accuracy at scale?
flashcards.a: Run the cheap linear model on all traffic, route only low-confidence or specifically-hard-category items to a more expensive fine-tuned transformer for a second pass -- captures most of the accuracy gain at a fraction of the full-transformer infrastructure cost.
